To initiate desorption, the bed must be heated while a vacuum pump directs the desorbed water and carbon dioxide to the product line. Bed heating was performed using hot water exchange through internal tubes, as modeled in Aspen Adsorption. As shown in Figure 37A, the temperature distribution is nearly uniform across three key points in the bed—front, middle, and outlet. Heating was conducted at a vacuum pressure of 0.2 bar, a practical level achievable in industrial-scale systems. Figure 38 presents the variation in CO₂ recovery and product purity as a function of desorption temperature. As shown, product purity remains above 99.5%, while recovery increases with higher desorption temperatures. Specifically, desorption at 100°C and 0.2 bar for 30 min results in a CO₂ recovery of approximately 84.71% at a purity of ~99.7%. These data form the basis of the TEA where the desorbed amount is used to determine the required catalyst and the adsorption air. Figure 37.
